explain.intro: Step 6 asks when to treat the immune response itself. The negative trial explains the caution; the ESC list says where it is still used.
why: **Myocarditis Treatment Trial (NEJM 1995): 111 patients with myocarditis and LVEF <45%, randomised to conventional therapy alone or with 24 weeks of immunosuppression.** Prednisone with cyclosporine or azathioprine did not improve LVEF or survival; it included virus-positive and virus-negative patients alike, since PCR was not used. Later virus-negative trials (TIMIC: prednisone plus azathioprine for 6 months) did improve LVEF.

**Worsening heart failure despite standard treatment; giant-cell or eosinophilic myocarditis, sarcoidosis; myocarditis with autoimmune disease.** These are the virus-negative immune forms. ESC 2025 says immunosuppressants and corticosteroids should not be used as initial therapy; it reserves them for biopsy-proven or highly suspected immune forms (giant-cell, eosinophilic, sarcoid, autoimmune), fulminant non-infectious myocarditis (IIa C) and refractory ventricular dysfunction (IIb C).

**Started only after active infection has been ruled out on EMB by PCR.** Suppressing immunity while a virus replicates removes the defence that limits myocyte lysis. Patient selection is the likely reason the unselected MTT was negative while the virus-negative TIMIC was positive (CVS-30, 43).
mimic: Myocarditis Treatment Trial vs TIMIC
MTT: unselected histological myocarditis, no benefit. TIMIC: virus-negative inflammatory cardiomyopathy, LVEF improved.
traps: “The Myocarditis Treatment Trial showed immunosuppression improves LVEF”
It did not; benefit appears only when patients are selected by a negative viral PCR.
decode: [pattern] Absolute precondition before immunosuppression in myocarditis?
Active infection excluded by PCR on endomyocardial biopsy.
explain.punch: Unselected immunosuppression failed in the Myocarditis Treatment Trial; it works only in virus-negative immune forms, above all giant-cell and eosinophilic myocarditis, so a negative PCR on biopsy comes first.

steps.q: **IE organism by setting:** name the likely bug.
steps.a:
**SETTING** | **ORGANISM**
Acute (days, sepsis, new severe regurgitation, Janeway lesions) | **S. aureus**: commonest overall (~30%), also on rheumatic/damaged valves
IVDU, right-sided (tricuspid) | **S. aureus**; less often Pseudomonas, Candida
Subacute on damaged native valve, after dental work | **Viridans streptococci**
Elderly after GU/GI procedure | **Enterococci** (E. faecalis); S. gallolyticus (bovis) → colonoscopy
Early prosthetic valve (<12 months) | **CoNS**, S. aureus, Gram-negatives, Candida
Blood culture-negative | Prior antibiotics (commonest); **HACEK**, Coxiella, Bartonella, Brucella, Tropheryma

explain.sub: Infective endocarditis → Recognition → Organism by setting
explain.intro: Step 1 starts with the organism, because the setting predicts it before cultures return and the organism then sets the tempo, the complications and the regimen. The bank question behind this card gives a rheumatic valve with five days of fever and shock, and only a fifth of the cohort chose S. aureus.
why: **Acute (days, sepsis, new severe regurgitation, Janeway lesions) → S. aureus: commonest overall (~30%), also on rheumatic or damaged valves.** S. aureus binds both normal and damaged endothelium through surface adhesins and destroys a leaflet within days. The tempo outweighs the substrate: a rheumatic valve does not make it streptococcal when the course is five days and the patient needs pressors.

**IVDU, right-sided (tricuspid) → S. aureus; less often Pseudomonas, Candida.** Skin flora is injected straight into the venous return to the tricuspid valve; contaminated water and diluents bring Pseudomonas and Candida.

**Subacute on a damaged native valve after dental work → viridans streptococci.** They need a ready-made fibrin–platelet nidus on an abnormal valve and are not destructive, so they cause weeks of low-grade fever, not shock.

**Elderly after a GU or GI procedure → enterococci (E. faecalis); S. gallolyticus (bovis) → colonoscopy.** S. gallolyticus bacteraemia is linked to colonic neoplasia, so the colon is examined even without bowel symptoms.

**Early prosthetic valve (<12 months) → CoNS, S. aureus, Gram-negatives, Candida.** These are acquired around the operation or in hospital and live in biofilm on the sewing ring. After 12 months the spectrum returns to that of native-valve IE.

**Blood culture-negative → prior antibiotics (commonest); HACEK, Coxiella, Bartonella, Brucella, Tropheryma.** These are fastidious or intracellular organisms that grow slowly or not at all in routine bottles, so they are found by serology, PCR or valve tissue (IE-15).
mimic: S. aureus vs viridans streptococci
Days, shock and a newly destroyed valve vs weeks of low-grade fever on an already abnormal valve.
Early vs late PVE
Under 12 months: hospital organisms (CoNS, S. aureus, Gram-negatives, Candida); later: the native-valve spectrum.
traps: “Rheumatic valve, so viridans streptococcus” (DocT GT2o Q124: only 20% chose S. aureus)
The predisposition tells you where IE settles, not which organism. Five days of fever, Janeway lesions, a newly severe MR and rising pressors are the S. aureus tempo.
“CoNS in the blood after valve surgery is a contaminant”
On a prosthetic valve within a year it is a leading cause, and Duke-ISCVID counts CoNS as a typical organism when intracardiac prosthetic material is present.
decode: Rheumatic MS, 5 days of fever, plantar lesions, newly severe MR, rising pressors: most likely organism? [DocT GT2o Q124, 20%]
S. aureus: an acute, destructive course whatever the substrate.
Fever and positive cultures 3 weeks after valve replacement: likely organism? [pattern]
CoNS or S. aureus (early PVE).
explain.punch: The tempo names the organism: days and destruction mean S. aureus, weeks on a damaged valve mean viridans streptococci, and the first year after valve surgery means hospital organisms.

steps.q:
**Duke-ISCVID 2023 criteria:**
a Major
b Minor
c Definite vs possible
steps.a:
a **Major**:
- **Micro**: *typical* organism (S. aureus, S. lugdunensis, E. faecalis, streptococci except pneumoniae/pyogenes, HACEK, Gemella, Abiotrophia, Granulicatella) in **≥2 sets**; *non-typical* (e.g. E. coli) in **≥3 sets**; Coxiella phase I IgG **>1:800**; Bartonella IgG ≥1:800; positive PCR
- **Imaging**: vegetation, abscess, perforation, pseudoaneurysm, fistula, new dehiscence on echo/**cardiac CT**; **PET-CT** uptake at a valve/graft/lead (>3 months after surgery); **new** regurgitation on echo
- **Surgical**: IE seen at operation
b **Minor**: predisposition (prosthesis, prior IE, RHD, IVDU, CIED, HCM, congenital), **fever >38 °C**, **vascular** (emboli, septic lung infarcts, cerebral/splenic abscess, mycotic aneurysm, ICH, Janeway), **immunological** (Osler, Roth, RF, immune-complex GN), **micro** not meeting major
c **Definite** = 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor. **Possible** = 1 major + 1 minor, or 3 minor.

explain.intro: Step 2 is proof. The 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria turn the bedside picture into ‘definite’, ‘possible’ or ‘rejected’; the bank questions test the thresholds (how many sets, which organism, how to count), not the list.
why: **Major: typical organism in ≥2 sets, non-typical (e.g. E. coli) in ≥3; Coxiella phase I IgG >1:800; Bartonella IgG ≥1:800; positive PCR; imaging (vegetation, abscess, perforation, pseudoaneurysm, fistula, new dehiscence on echo or cardiac CT; PET-CT uptake >3 months after surgery; new regurgitation on echo); IE seen at operation.** The typical organisms are so specific for IE that two sets are enough; anything else needs three to exclude contamination or another source. With intracardiac prosthetic material, ISCVID also counts CoNS, Corynebacterium striatum/jeikeium, Serratia, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Cutibacterium, M. chimaera and Candida as typical. PET-CT within 3 months of surgery is only minor, because healing tissue around the sewing ring takes up FDG too.

**Minor: predisposition (prosthesis, prior IE, RHD, IVDU, CIED, HCM, congenital), fever >38 °C, vascular, immunological, microbiology not meeting major.** ISCVID words the valve predisposition as ‘more than mild regurgitation or stenosis of any cause’, which is why rheumatic MS/MR counts. A culture that fails the major threshold is not discarded; it becomes a minor criterion (IE-04).

**Definite = 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor; possible = 1 major + 1 minor, or 3 minor.** Definite can also be pathological (organisms or active IE in a vegetation, valve or embolus). ‘Rejected’ needs a firm alternative diagnosis, resolution (or no IE at surgery or autopsy) after under 4 days of antibiotics, or failure to reach ‘possible’.
mimic: Duke-ISCVID 2023 vs modified Duke (2000)
2023 adds cardiac CT and PET-CT as major imaging, the surgical criterion, PCR, and CIED/HCM/IVDU predispositions; the arithmetic for definite and possible is unchanged.
PET-CT major vs minor
More than 3 months after implantation: major; within 3 months: minor.
traps: “Worsening of a known murmur is a major criterion”
Only new regurgitation on echo is major; worsening of existing regurgitation does not count, and a new murmur on auscultation is minor and only when echo is unavailable.
“Any organism in two sets is major”
Two sets only for typical organisms; E. coli and other rare causes need three.
decode: Count majors and minors and classify (definite, possible, rejected) [DocT GT6 Q3; worked in IE-04]
2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor = definite.
Which imaging became a major criterion in 2023? [pattern]
Cardiac CT, and [18F]FDG PET-CT more than 3 months after surgery.
explain.punch: Two sets for a typical organism, three for a rare one; a culture that fails as major still counts as minor; definite is two major, one major plus three minor, or five minor.

steps.q:
**Embolic and immune complications of IE:**
a Where emboli go and what they look like
b Embolic risk factors
c Immune complications
steps.a:
a **Brain** (~20–40%): stroke, **multiple ring-enhancing abscesses** at grey-white junction (IVDU + fever + hemiparesis), **mycotic aneurysm** → ICH/SAH. **Spleen**: infarct or abscess. **Lung**: septic emboli from right-sided IE. Limbs, kidney, mesentery, coronary.
b **Vegetation >10 mm** (>30 mm very high), **mobile**, **mitral** (anterior leaflet), **S. aureus**, Candida, prior embolism; risk highest before and in the **first 2 weeks** of antibiotics.
c **Immune-complex GN** (red-cell casts, low complement), Osler nodes, Roth spots, arthritis, positive RF.

explain.sub: Infective endocarditis → Complications → Emboli and immune phenomena
explain.intro: Step 3: what the vegetation does once it is there. It throws fragments into the circulation and keeps releasing antigen into the blood; the bank questions give the embolic or immune picture and ask for the one diagnosis behind it.
why: **Brain (~20–40%): stroke, multiple ring-enhancing abscesses at the grey–white junction, mycotic aneurysm → ICH/SAH; spleen: infarct or abscess; lung: septic emboli from right-sided IE; also limbs, kidney, mesentery, coronary.** Left-sided fragments go wherever arterial flow takes them, and the brain is the commonest symptomatic target; emboli lodge where arteries narrow, at the grey–white junction. An infected embolus in a distal artery weakens its wall and forms a mycotic aneurysm, which can bleed.

**Embolic risk: vegetation >10 mm (>30 mm very high), mobile, mitral (anterior leaflet), S. aureus, Candida, prior embolism; highest before and in the first 2 weeks of antibiotics.** Effective therapy sterilises and organises the vegetation, so risk falls steeply after two weeks; that is why surgery to prevent embolism is decided early (IE-08).

**Immune complications: immune-complex GN (red-cell casts, low complement), Osler nodes, Roth spots, arthritis, positive RF.** Continuous antigen release forms circulating immune complexes that deposit in glomeruli (consuming complement), skin and retina.
mimic: Osler nodes vs Janeway lesions
Painful pulp nodules (immunological minor) vs painless palmar or plantar macules (vascular minor).
IE vs systemic vasculitis
Fever, a murmur, positive cultures and emboli point to IE; vasculitis does not make vegetations.
traps: “Vasculitis” for IVDU + apical murmur + stroke + red-cell casts (Marrow QB25-Q28)
Septic emboli and immune-complex GN from left-sided (mitral) IE explain every finding.
“Tuberculoma or glioma” for multiple ring-enhancing lesions in a febrile heroin user (DocT Substance-Related (Part 1) Q18, 87%)
Multiple lesions with acute fever and hemiparesis are septic embolic abscesses; tuberculoma is subacute and usually single or few.
decode: IVDU, fever, apical murmur, stroke, red-cell casts: cause? [Marrow QB25-Q28]
Septic emboli from IE.
RHD, fever, arthralgia, confusion: suspect? [Marrow QB23-Q12]
Acute infective endocarditis.
IV heroin, fever, altered sensorium, hemiparesis, multiple ring-enhancing lesions [DocT Substance-Related (Part 1) Q18, 87%]
Brain abscesses from septic emboli of IE.
explain.punch: A fever with emboli in several beds plus nephritis is one disease: the vegetation throws fragments and immune complexes, most dangerously in the first two weeks.

steps.q: **Aortic-valve IE on day 3 of correct antibiotics develops new PR prolongation, then Mobitz II (or complete heart block), still febrile. Meaning and next step?**
steps.a:
- New AV block = **perivalvular (aortic-root) abscess** eroding the conduction system near the AV node/His bundle
- **TEE** to define abscess, fistula, pseudoaneurysm
- **Urgent surgery** (within **3–5 days**): locally uncontrolled infection; antibiotics cannot sterilise an abscess
- Temporary pacing as needed
- Daily ECG in aortic IE to catch it early

explain.sub: Infective endocarditis → Complications → New heart block = root abscess
explain.intro: Step 3 also covers spread beyond the leaflet. Two bank questions give new heart block in endocarditis and offer ‘continue antibiotics’ or ‘wait 6 weeks’. The parts follow the card’s bullets.
why: **New AV block = perivalvular (aortic-root) abscess eroding the conduction system near the AV node/His bundle.** The His bundle runs under the membranous septum, beneath the commissure between the non-coronary and right coronary cusps, so infection spreading from the aortic annulus there blocks conduction. New block in aortic IE is a specific marker of abscess, though many abscesses never cause it.
**TEE to define abscess, fistula, pseudoaneurysm.** TTE misses about half of root abscesses; ESC 2023 asks for repeat imaging (TEE, or cardiac CT) whenever a new complication is suspected.

**Urgent surgery (within 3–5 days): locally uncontrolled infection; antibiotics cannot sterilise an abscess.** A pus cavity has no blood supply, so drugs do not reach it and fever persists. ESC 2023 makes this a Class I urgent indication, native or prosthetic.

**Temporary pacing as needed; daily ECG in aortic IE to catch it early.** Mobitz II and complete block are infranodal and unstable. ESC 2023 also advises epicardial pacing at surgery when complete block is present with a predictor that it will persist.
mimic: Root abscess vs drug-induced AV block
Abscess: aortic IE, still febrile, progressive block; drugs (beta-blocker, digoxin, calcium-channel blocker): no fever, no new echo lesion.
traps: “Continue antibiotics alone” or “delay surgery 6 weeks” (DocT CGT6 Q118; Marrow QB25-Q10)
Heart block with an abscess and persistent fever is uncontrolled infection: urgent surgery, Class I.
decode: Aortic IE, day 3 of correct antibiotics, new Mobitz II: next step? [Marrow QB25-Q10]
Surgical referral (root abscess).
PVE, complete heart block, periannular abscess on TEE, still febrile: management? [DocT CGT6 Q118]
Urgent valve surgery.
explain.punch: In aortic endocarditis, new AV block means the infection has burrowed into the root beside the His bundle; image it with TEE and send for urgent surgery, because no antibiotic reaches an abscess.

steps.q: **ESC 2023 surgery indications in left-sided IE, by timing:**
steps.a:
**TIMING** | **INDICATION**
**Emergency (<24 h)** | **HF with cardiogenic shock or pulmonary oedema** from severe acute regurgitation, obstruction or fistula
**Urgent (3–5 days)** | HF without shock; **locally uncontrolled infection** (abscess, pseudoaneurysm, fistula, enlarging vegetation, new AV block)
**Urgent** | **Fungal** or multiresistant organism; **persistent bacteraemia** despite correct antibiotics and source control
**Urgent** | **Vegetation ≥10 mm + ≥1 embolic event** on antibiotics (Class I)
**Urgent (IIa)** | Vegetation ≥10 mm + severe valve disease and low risk; vegetation **≥30 mm**; S. aureus or non-HACEK Gram-negative PVE

explain.sub: Infective endocarditis → Surgery → ESC 2023 indications by timing
explain.intro: Step 4: when antibiotics are not enough. ESC 2023 groups indications by reason (heart failure, uncontrolled infection, embolism) and timing (emergency <24 h, urgent 3–5 days, non-urgent during the same admission). The parts follow the table’s rows.
why: **Emergency (<24 h): HF with cardiogenic shock or pulmonary oedema from severe acute regurgitation, obstruction or fistula.** This is a mechanical failure that no drug can fix, so the length of antibiotic treatment does not matter (IE-07).

**Urgent (3–5 days): HF without shock; locally uncontrolled infection (abscess, pseudoaneurysm, fistula, enlarging vegetation, new AV block).** ESC 2023 defines ‘urgent’ as 3–5 days (2015 said only ‘within a few days’). Walled-off infection is not reached by antibiotics (IE-06).

**Urgent: fungal or multiresistant organism; persistent bacteraemia despite correct antibiotics and source control.** Fungal and multiresistant IE are surgical because medical cure is rare (IE-15). ESC 2023 grades persistent positive cultures for more than a week, after metastatic foci are controlled, as ‘should be considered’ (IIa).

**Urgent: vegetation ≥10 mm + ≥1 embolic event on antibiotics (Class I).** Also Class I: a vegetation ≥10 mm with any other surgical indication. Embolic risk is highest early (IE-05), so the decision cannot wait for the course to finish.

**Urgent (IIa): vegetation ≥10 mm + severe valve disease and low risk; vegetation ≥30 mm; S. aureus or non-HACEK Gram-negative PVE.** Only the last is still IIa in ESC 2023 (‘should be considered’, IIa C): these organisms rarely clear from prosthetic material. The vegetation rows are 2015 wording. In 2023 a vegetation ≥10 mm with any other surgical indication, which takes in severe valve disease, was upgraded to Class I; the separate 30 mm cut-off was dropped; and an isolated vegetation ≥10 mm without embolism or severe dysfunction, in a low-risk patient, ‘may be considered’ (IIb B; 2015 set this at >15 mm, IIb C).
mimic: Left- vs right-sided IE surgery
Tricuspid IE is usually medical; ESC 2023 operates for RV failure from acute severe TR, recurrent pulmonary emboli needing ventilation, residual vegetation >20 mm, or left-sided involvement.
traps: “Add a second antibiotic” for MRSA aortic IE with a splenic embolus on day 2 (Marrow QB25-Q24)
Embolism with a vegetation is a surgical question: cardiothoracic opinion now.
“Finish 6 weeks of antibiotics before operating”
Emergency and urgent timings run from the indication, not the course; operating on active infection is accepted.
decode: MRSA aortic IE, splenic lesion on day 2: next step? [Marrow QB25-Q24]
Cardiothoracic surgery consult for septic embolus.
Mechanical mitral valve, candidaemia, EF 35%: next step? [Marrow QB25-Q35]
Antifungal plus early surgery (IE-15).
Which IE indication needs surgery within 24 h? [pattern]
Refractory pulmonary oedema or cardiogenic shock from valve failure.
explain.punch: Operate within 24 hours for shock or oedema from a failed valve, within 3–5 days for heart failure, uncontrolled infection or a ≥10 mm vegetation that has embolised; antibiotics do not change those clocks.

steps.q: **Empirical antibiotics for IE (ESC 2023), cultures pending:**
steps.a:
**SETTING** | **REGIMEN**
Community NVE or **late PVE (≥12 months)** | **Ampicillin + ceftriaxone**, or ampicillin + (flu)cloxacillin + gentamicin
Penicillin allergy | Vancomycin + ceftriaxone
**Early PVE (<12 months)** or healthcare-associated | **Vancomycin** (or daptomycin) + **gentamicin** + **rifampicin** (rifampicin only for PVE)
Culture-negative early PVE (AHA) | Vancomycin + gentamicin + **cefepime** + rifampicin
Narrow | Switch to organism-specific therapy once cultures return

explain.intro: Step 5 begins before the organism is known: the regimen follows the setting, the same split as IE-01. The parts follow the table’s rows.
why: **Community NVE or late PVE (≥12 months): ampicillin + ceftriaxone, or ampicillin + (flu)cloxacillin + gentamicin.** This covers streptococci, enterococci (ampicillin + ceftriaxone act together, IE-13), HACEK (ceftriaxone) and, with cloxacillin, MSSA. ESC 2023 grades it IIa.
**Penicillin allergy: vancomycin + ceftriaxone.** The ESC 2023 table lists cefazolin or vancomycin with gentamicin (IIb) for this group; see FLAGS.

**Early PVE (<12 months) or healthcare-associated: vancomycin (or daptomycin) + gentamicin + rifampicin (rifampicin only for PVE).** Vancomycin covers MRSA and CoNS; rifampicin penetrates biofilm on prosthetic material but, given alone into a high inoculum, selects resistance, so ESC 2023 adds it after 3–5 days of effective therapy.
**Culture-negative early PVE (AHA): vancomycin + gentamicin + cefepime + rifampicin.** Cefepime adds the hospital Gram-negatives that the ESC early-PVE regimen leaves to gentamicin.

**Narrow to organism-specific therapy once cultures return.** In stable patients a later step-down to oral therapy is allowed: in POET (left-sided IE with streptococci, E. faecalis, S. aureus or CoNS, after ≥10 days IV) oral was non-inferior (composite 9.0% vs 12.1% at 6 months) and better at a median of 3.5 years. ESC 2023 asks for a TEE showing no progression before the switch.
mimic: Early vs late PVE regimen
Early: vancomycin-based with rifampicin and Gram-negative cover; late: the community native-valve regimen.
traps: “Vancomycin + ceftriaxone” 4 weeks after mechanical AVR with negative cultures (DocT CGT5 Q56)

Ceftriaxone misses Pseudomonas and many hospital Gram-negatives, and the pair has neither gentamicin nor rifampicin; early PVE needs MRSA, CoNS, biofilm and resistant Gram-negative cover: vancomycin, cefepime, gentamicin, rifampicin (AHA 2015).
“Rifampicin from day 1”
Added after 3–5 days, once the bacteraemia is controlled, or resistance emerges.
decode: Fever and heart failure 4 weeks after mechanical AVR, cultures negative after antibiotics: broadest recommended empirical cover? [DocT CGT5 Q56]
Vancomycin, cefepime, gentamicin, rifampicin.
Which IE patients may step down to oral antibiotics? [pattern]
Stable left-sided IE after ≥10 days IV with no complication on TEE (POET).
explain.punch: Empirical cover follows the setting: ampicillin plus ceftriaxone for community and late prosthetic IE, vancomycin-based with gentamicin and later rifampicin for early prosthetic IE.

steps.q:
**S. aureus IE (not CRBSI) regimens, ESC 2023:**
a MSSA native valve
b MRSA or true penicillin anaphylaxis
c Prosthetic valve
d Uncomplicated right-sided MSSA in IVDU
steps.a:
a **(Flu)cloxacillin 12 g/day** in 4–6 doses (oxacillin/nafcillin) **or cefazolin 6 g/day** in 3 doses, **4–6 weeks**; **no gentamicin**
b **Vancomycin** 30–60 mg/kg/day (AUC 400–600) **or daptomycin 10 mg/kg/day**, 4–6 weeks
c Anti-staphylococcal agent + **rifampicin** (≥6 weeks) + **gentamicin 2 weeks**
d **2 weeks** of (flu)cloxacillin can suffice

explain.sub: Infective endocarditis → Antibiotics → S. aureus regimens
explain.intro: Step 5 for the commonest and most lethal organism. The DocT question behind this card offers vancomycin because it ‘covers everything’; for MSSA that is the wrong reason.
why: **MSSA native valve: (flu)cloxacillin 12 g/day in 4–6 doses (oxacillin/nafcillin) or cefazolin 6 g/day in 3 doses, 4–6 weeks; no gentamicin.** Beta-lactams kill MSSA faster than vancomycin, and MSSA treated with vancomycin fails and kills more often. ESC 2023 does not recommend aminoglycosides in staphylococcal native-valve IE: no benefit, more kidney injury.

**MRSA or true penicillin anaphylaxis: vancomycin 30–60 mg/kg/day (AUC 400–600) or daptomycin 10 mg/kg/day, 4–6 weeks.** ESC uses the high daptomycin dose (10 mg/kg) and advises a second agent with it (for example cloxacillin or fosfomycin) to prevent resistance. Daptomycin is inactivated by surfactant, so it fails in alveolar pneumonia; septic pulmonary emboli from right-sided IE are not a contraindication.

**Prosthetic valve: anti-staphylococcal agent + rifampicin (≥6 weeks) + gentamicin 2 weeks.** Rifampicin is the drug that acts in biofilm; it starts after 3–5 days of effective therapy to avoid resistance.

**Uncomplicated right-sided MSSA in IVDU: 2 weeks of (flu)cloxacillin can suffice.** ESC conditions: MSSA with a prompt clinical response, vegetation <20 mm, no metastatic infection, no left-sided or prosthetic involvement, no severe immunosuppression, and not with a glycopeptide.
mimic: Cefazolin vs ceftriaxone for MSSA
Cefazolin is an anti-staphylococcal first-choice drug; ceftriaxone is weaker against staphylococci.
traps: “Vancomycin” for MSSA mitral IE with septic emboli and HF (DocT Antimicrobials Q5, 61%)
Vancomycin kills MSSA slowly and penetrates vegetations poorly; oxacillin or nafcillin (or cefazolin) wins.
“Add gentamicin to MSSA native-valve IE”
No benefit and more AKI; gentamicin belongs only to the prosthetic-valve regimen.
decode: MSSA mitral IE, multiple septic emboli, worsening HF: most appropriate initial regimen? [DocT Antimicrobials Q5, 61%]
Oxacillin or nafcillin.
Right-sided MSSA IE in an IVDU, prompt response, vegetation 12 mm: duration? [pattern]
2 weeks of (flu)cloxacillin can suffice.
explain.punch: MSSA is treated with an anti-staphylococcal beta-lactam, never vancomycin by choice; gentamicin and rifampicin belong only to prosthetic-valve S. aureus.

steps.q:
**Enterococcal IE:**
a E. faecalis, no HLAR, normal kidneys
b HLAR or renal risk
c Beta-lactam allergy
d VRE faecium
steps.a:
a **Ampicillin/amoxicillin + gentamicin**: **4 weeks** NVE, **6 weeks** PVE or symptoms >3 months (gentamicin may be limited to 2 weeks)
b **Ampicillin + ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly × 6 weeks** (ESC 2023 Class I; avoids nephrotoxicity)
c **Vancomycin + gentamicin × 6 weeks**
d **High-dose daptomycin** (10–12 mg/kg) + ampicillin or fosfomycin; linezolid alternative

explain.intro: Step 5: enterococci are slow to kill, so the question is always which partner to give with ampicillin, and for how long.
why: **E. faecalis, no HLAR, normal kidneys: ampicillin/amoxicillin + gentamicin, 4 weeks NVE, 6 weeks PVE or symptoms >3 months (gentamicin may be limited to 2 weeks).** Ampicillin alone only inhibits enterococci; gentamicin, let in through the damaged wall, adds the killing.

**HLAR or renal risk: ampicillin + ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly × 6 weeks (ESC 2023 Class I; avoids nephrotoxicity).** Ceftriaxone saturates PBP2/3 while ampicillin binds PBP4/5, so together they kill without an aminoglycoside, and ESC accepts it for non-HLAR strains too.
**Beta-lactam allergy: vancomycin + gentamicin × 6 weeks.** It is the only combination left that kills, at the cost of two nephrotoxins.

**VRE faecium: high-dose daptomycin (10–12 mg/kg) + ampicillin or fosfomycin; linezolid alternative.** E. faecium is usually ampicillin-resistant and intrinsically ceftriaxone-resistant; daptomycin is bactericidal, and a partner prevents daptomycin resistance.
mimic: E. faecalis vs E. faecium
Faecalis: ampicillin-susceptible, ampicillin + ceftriaxone works; faecium: often ampicillin- and vancomycin-resistant, daptomycin-based.
traps: “Amoxicillin + ceftriaxone for 4 weeks” (DocT GrandT1 Q95, 41%)
The combination is right but the course is 6 weeks; with only 4 weeks offered, ampicillin + gentamicin for 6 weeks is the best available answer.
“Ampicillin” or “tigecycline” for VRE faecium bacteraemia in shock (DocT Antimicrobials Q14, 58%)
Faecium is usually ampicillin-resistant and tigecycline is bacteriostatic with low blood levels; daptomycin.
decode: E. faecalis IE, penicillin MIC 4 mg/L, no HLAR: initial regimen? [DocT GrandT1 Q95, 41%]
Ampicillin + gentamicin for 6 weeks.
VRE faecium bacteraemia, ventilated, on vasopressors: agent? [DocT Antimicrobials Q14, 58%]
Daptomycin.
explain.punch: Enterococci need two drugs to die: ampicillin with gentamicin, or ampicillin with ceftriaxone for 6 weeks when the kidneys or HLAR forbid gentamicin; faecium needs daptomycin.
